newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parking-lot firm thrives on pockets of land.
newsitem.headline: Japan parking-lot firm thrives on pockets of land.

text.p: Navigating the congested, narrow streets of Tokyo is easy compared to the headache of hunting for a place to park.
But one firm is trying to change all that -- by transforming tiny pockets of land into parking lots.

Apart from the increase in drivers happy about not having to pay parking tickets and a decrease in drivers frustrated by illegally parked cars blocking roads, analysts say Park24 Co's business is turning out to be a success.

"The firm's profitability lies in the fact Japan's stagnant land market makes paying rent almost nothing in comparison to the profits the lots, which are almost always full, rake in," said Norio Sanada, analyst at Nikko Research Centre.
"Personnel costs are kept at a bare minimum as the lots are self-service."
Park24, which registered its shares for over-the-counter trade in late March, had a humble beginning as a vendor of "parking prohibited" sign boards and parking meters.

But in 1991, president Kiyoshi Nishikawa ventured into the world of parking lots, focusing on hidden pockets of land in cities. In little more than five years, the lots have come to generate over 80 percent of the firm's earnings.

As of end-March, the firm's parking facilities held about 17,000 cars, 40 percent of which are in or around Tokyo. The fee for the lots, which are mostly nestled between buildings, is set at 100 yen (about $0.80) per 15 to 20 minutes during the daytime, depending on the area, and 100 yen per hour at night.
"Our smallest lots park one car," a spokeswoman at Park24 said.
The unmanned lots have an automatic lock device which is activated once the timer is set. The car can only be released when the fee is paid.
Park24's parent current profit is expected to surge 45.6 percent from the previous year to 1.57 billion yen ($12.4 million) in the year to October 31, 1997.
Analysts predict a similar profit growth rate in the next few years, and sales are expected to soar 33.3 percent to 19.7 billion yen ($156 million) in 1997.

"In about two years we hope to increase the number of cars which can be parked on our lots to 24,000," Nishikawa told Reuters. "In addition to building lots on rented land, we also hope to buy land of our own and build car parks for about 5,000 cars."
The lots, until now, have been mainly built in cities but posh residential areas are also proving to be good sites.

"Housewives often visit their friends by car on their way home from the supermarket, but there are not many places to park, even in upper-class areas," one "Big Four" brokerage analyst said. "Business is brisk for short-term parking lots."

Nishikawa added the firm has ambitious plans to franchise the car park business as well as to develop a car navigation system to inform drivers of vacancies and provide advance reservations for parking space.
"We are on the brink of expansion and we should be able to increase annual sales by about five billion yen ($39.6 million)," he said.

Salomon Brothers analyst Tetusya Furumoto said government statistics show that there are only 2.4 million parking spaces for the 70 million cars in Japan, demonstrating the huge need for parking space. Park24's business should be secure in the medium to long term, he said.

"There is a risk that when land prices pick up, landlords will find find better ways to utilise their land," Furumoto added. "But the lots are built mainly on slivers of land wedged between buildings which can't be used for much else."
